h1: Moving from hospitality to brewery sales
title: Moving from Hospitality to Brewery Sales | Craft Beer School
desc: How bar and restaurant staff move into brewery sales in India, what carries over from hospitality and what you need to learn about beer and the trade.
teaser: You already know what bar managers want. Brewery sales pays you to use it.
standfirst: Bartenders, servers and restaurant managers make strong brewery sales people because they have stood on the other side of the deal. The move means adding product knowledge, territory discipline and an understanding of how beer reaches the outlet.
sections:
A brewery sales rep's customer is the outlet: the owner, the bar manager, the purchase team. If you have worked in hospitality, you know what these people care about: margins, reliable supply, beer that sells without fuss and support when something goes wrong on a Friday night.

You also know what annoys them: reps who arrive at peak hour, promise stock that never comes and vanish when a keg goes bad. That inside knowledge is the main reason breweries hire from hospitality. Our guide on brewery sales careers describes the wider role.

Equally, you know how a menu gets built and why some beers move while others gather dust. That understanding of guest behaviour is something FMCG sellers have to learn on the job.
Product knowledge is the gap to close

Hospitality staff often know how to sell a beer but not how it is made. In brewery sales you need both. Expect to explain the difference between a lager and an ale, why a wheat beer is hazy, what bitterness units mean on a menu and why an IPA should be drunk fresh.

You do not need to brew professionally. You need enough to train bar staff, handle questions from guests and talk confidently with brewers. Tasting skills help too: knowing the common off-flavours lets you spot a dirty line or an old keg before the customer blames the brewery. Our guide to beer off-flavours is a good place to start.

As a bartender you poured from the tap. As a brewery rep you look after what happens behind it. Draught lines must be cleaned regularly. Draught quality guidance commonly recommends at least every two weeks. Gas pressure must suit the beer and the line length. Beer should be held cold, usually around 2 to 4 °C, from keg to glass.

When a guest complains about a beer, the cause is often the system, not the beer. A rep who can check line cleaning records, gas pressure and cooler temperature politely keeps the account and protects the brand. That technical side is new for many people moving from hospitality.
Learn how beer reaches the outlet

In hospitality, beer simply arrived. In sales you learn the route. In India, alcohol is regulated mostly by states. Excise, pricing, outlet licences and distribution rules vary between states and change through notifications. In some states a government body handles wholesale. In others private distributors do.

That affects what you can offer an outlet and how orders flow. You will work with distributors, track kegs and handle stock rotation. Keep it simple at first: learn the rules in your own city and ask the company's regulatory team when in doubt.
Territory discipline is a new habit

Hospitality runs shift to shift. Sales runs on a weekly plan: which outlets to visit, what to check, what to sell in. Expect targets on volume, new outlets and sometimes collections. Expect to report what you did in a CRM or a shared sheet.

Many people from hospitality find this the hardest change. The fix is routine. Plan visits outside the outlet's busy hours, keep notes after every visit and follow up on everything you promised. Reliability is what bar managers remember.
Your hospitality network is worth a lot

Bar managers move between venues. Chefs open restaurants. The people you worked with will become your customers. Keep those contacts warm, professionally. A rep who can call a new venue's manager by name and say "we worked together at the old place" has a head start.

Be careful with conflicts though. If you are joining a brewery that competes with your current employer's supplier, leave your old job cleanly before talking business. To see the same job from the production side, our guide on moving from brewer to brewery sales shows what a brewer brings to it.

Next shift, ask whoever looks after the beer at your venue to show you the draught system: kegs, gas, coolers and lines. Ask when the lines were last cleaned and how. Then write a one paragraph description of each beer on your menu that you could use to train a new server. Bring both to your first sales interview.
faqs: Can bartenders move into brewery sales?
Yes, many do. Hospitality experience means you already understand outlet owners, bar managers and guests, which is the core of the job.
What do I need to learn for brewery sales?
How beer is made and how styles differ, draught quality basics, the state rules that shape distribution and the discipline of planning and reporting a territory.
What temperature should draught beer be held at?
Commonly around 2 to 4 °C from keg to glass. Warmer beer foams more on dispense and tastes less fresh.
Is a hospitality network useful in brewery sales?
Very. Former colleagues become customers as they move between venues. Keep those relationships professional and avoid conflicts of interest.
